# Debt sustainability

Debt is sustainable when a government can meet its debt obligations without restructuring, arrears, or a policy adjustment too large to be feasible. The official judgement comes from a debt sustainability analysis (DSA), which IMF and World Bank staff prepare for IMF programmes and regular IMF reviews (Article IV consultations) and publish in IMF country reports. A DSA is based on 10-year or longer projections, the whole public sector including domestic debt and guarantees, present values, stress tests, and staff judgement. The DFO supplies historical external debt stocks and flows, contractual projections of debt service, historical fiscal and external indicators from the World Development Indicators, and IMF projections of GDP only. Indicators built from them describe some of the pressures a DSA weighs, and none of its projected paths. Where an official rating exists, the DSA is the authority, and a different reading of the indicators comes from one of the differences below.

## Which framework applies

The IMF and World Bank assess low-income countries under the joint Debt Sustainability Framework for Low-Income Countries (LIC-DSF). The IMF assesses every other member under the Sovereign Risk and Debt Sustainability Framework for market-access countries (MAC-SRDSF). The IMF's list of LIC DSAs names the countries assessed under the LIC-DSF, with the latest rating, and members not on the list are assessed under the MAC-SRDSF, whatever its income group or World Bank lending category. Three countries are exceptions. Guyana is assessed under the LIC-DSF but is left off the list because it is not eligible for the IMF's concessional lending. Saint Lucia is eligible and is assessed under the MAC-SRDSF. Syria became eligible in 2024 and does not yet have a DSA. Market-access ratings appear only in each country's IMF report, and no table collects them. The DFO holds no market-access ratings, so a market-access country's official assessment is in its IMF report, outside the DFO. The two frameworks use different rating terms and scales, so ratings from different frameworks are not comparable, and a multi-country question spans both.

## Ratings and judgements

A DSA provides two outputs. The risk rating grades how likely debt-related stress is. The LIC-DSF rates it low, moderate, high, or in debt distress, and the MAC-SRDSF rates it low, moderate, or high for each time horizon. The sustainability judgement asks whether the stress can be resolved without restructuring. They answer different questions. Most countries rated at high risk on the IMF's LIC list have debt assessed as sustainable, and a country in debt distress can have sustainable debt when the distress reflects arrears it is clearing.

Solvency assesses whether the debt stock is too large for the economy to carry, measured by debt against GDP or exports. Liquidity assesses whether payments coming due can be met, measured by debt service against exports or revenue, financing needs, and reserves. A solvent country can face a liquidity crisis; for example, a large Eurobond coming due when markets are closed to it.

Default depends on market access, IMF programmes, and political decisions outside the indicators, and no framework predicts it.

## Public-data indicators against DSA indicators

Indicators built from external debt data and IMF macroeconomic data differ from a DSA's for several reasons.

- Face value against present value. The LIC-DSF's external solvency indicator is in present value, which the debt-concepts skill covers.
- History against projections. DSA risk signals come from projected paths over 10 years, so a historical ratio above a threshold describes the past. The DFO has no fiscal or growth projections, so it cannot trace a projected debt path.
- Revenue. The LIC-DSF divides by revenue excluding grants. Revenue including grants yields a lower ratio for grant-dependent countries.
- Coverage. A DSA covers state-owned enterprises, guarantees, and domestic debt where data allow. External debt data miss some of this, and the IMF's government finance figures cover only the central government for some countries.
- Interest. The World Development Indicators report central government interest payments as a share of revenue, narrower coverage than a DSA's public debt.

Timing. A DSA can predate the latest data by years, and its rating reflects the conditions that existed when it was prepared. A rating's date matters as much as the rating. The list carries ratings from 2014 to 2026, and conditions can change well before a new DSA, as when debt later found to have been misreported changes the picture.
